newsitem.title: USA: After spring lull, consumers spend more in June.
newsitem.headline: After spring lull, consumers spend more in June.

text.p: Retailers rang up their first increase in sales in four months during June, the Commerce Department said on Tuesday, as consumers spent more freely after a spring lull.
Total retail sales increased 0.5 percent to a seasonally adjusted $210.3 billion -- helped by a surprising pickup in new-car sales -- after a revised 0.3 percent drop in May.

Analysts said the June increase reflected a modest revival in consumer demand, enough to fuel continued economic growth but not brisk enough to fan fears of inflationary price rises that might prompt dampening interest-rate rises.

"The second quarter clearly was a payback quarter for the extremely strong first-quarter spending, but there are indications we came out of the second quarter on a steepening trend," said Robert Dederick, economic consultant to Northern Trust Co. in Chicago.
"It's not explosive by any means," he added. "But as the weather warmed, consumers' spending propensities seemed to warm as well."

Financial markets took the report in stride, focusing on its indication that April and May were even weaker than previously reported. Bond prices dipped after the figures were published but largely recovered after dealers decided they were not a harbinger of increased inflation pressures.

May sales originally were reported down 0.1 percent but that was revised to a steeper decline while April sales, previously reported falling 0.9 percent, instead dropped a revised 1.1 percent. March sales fell 0.3 percent.

Commerce said that June sales by new-car dealers climbed 1.1 percent to $50.4 billion after a 1.2 percent May fall. That was a surprise since automakers earlier reported feeble June sales that were expected to be a drag on overall retail business.
Excluding new cars, June retail sales rose a relatively modest 0.3 percent after being flat in May and declining 0.6 percent in April.

Analysts said dealers may have been selling cars from their inventories in June, whereas earlier reports of weaker sales came from carmakers themselves, some of whom were hurt by strikes that held down production earlier this year.
The overall trend in retail sales was firm in June.

Sales of all types of durable goods, from cars to refrigerators and furniture, rose 0.5 percent to $85.1 billion after a 0.9 percent fall in May. Sales of non-durables like food and clothing were up 0.4 percent last month to $125.2 billion after rising 0.1 percent in May.

"The modest rise in June retail sales suggests that the slump in household spending may have ended and consumption expenditures are rising at a moderate pace as the economy heads into the third quarter," said Joel Naroff, Philadelphia-based economist for First Union Corp. in Charlotte, N.C.

Sales by general merchandise stores rose 0.8 percent to $27.5 billion following a 0.5 percent gain in May. At apparel stores, clothing sales were flat in June at $9.6 billion but that was after a sturdy 1.2 percent jump in May.
Strong job growth and rising incomes are widely expected to lead to a recovery in consumer spending that fuels two-thirds of national economic activity.

"The extent of the rebound will be the key in determining Federal Reserve policy," Naroff noted. The Fed last raised short-term interest rates a quarter percentage point on March 25, citing strong demand that it said raised inflation risks.

U.S. central bank policy-makers are next scheduled to meet Aug. 19 to consider interest-rate strategy. The Fed held rates steady at its past two policy-setting sessions in May and July amid signs inflation was muted to nonexistent.

After shooting ahead at a booming 5.9 percent annual rate in the first quarter, economic growth measured by gross domestic product is widely forecast to have slowed to a rate around 2 percent to 2.5 percent in the quarter ended June 30.
Dederick said he third-quarter GDP likely will advance at a 3.3 percent annual rate, but emphasised it "depends crucially upon the consumer" maintaining moderate spending momentum.
Some categories of goods posted sales declines in June.
Sales of building materials fell 1.2 percent in June to $11.9 billion after a 0.1 percent decline in May.
Gasoline service station sales decreased 0.9 percent to $12.7 billion after falling 2 percent in May. But the sales figures may reflect recent declines in gasoline prices.
